summary:
Región del Maule stands under the national framework of Chile, where legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis under Gender Identity Law 21.120 (introduced 2013, enacted 2018, operative 2019). People aged 14 and over can change their name and sex on all official documents without therapy or sex-reassignment surgery, so a traveller's identity papers can be made to match their presentation. Birth certificates also offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Family and equality law at national level provides that same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since 10 March 2022, on a law approved 9 December 2021, following civil unions available since 2015. The 2012 Zamudio anti-discrimination law protects sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and allows individuals to file anti-discrimination lawsuits. Since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences, and in 2025 a criminal court issued the country's first lesbophobic-femicide conviction under Article 390 ter of the penal code.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations, and rules on access for trans visitors. A standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitors implementation.

No region-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding exists for Región del Maule; its recorded profile comes from the shared national case table, in which its 2024 share of national LGBTIQ+ discrimination cases was 1.56%. A low share is not evidence of safety, because national case numbers rose in 2025 to their highest recorded level.

Documented violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.
tangentialFactors:
The policy record has stalled nationally. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 the first year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity in Chile, covering 2025 and published in March 2026, describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

Restrictions now target trans children's care. Congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, a health-ministry circular numbered N8 restricts PAIG for minors, and legislative initiative CEI-57 is directed against the rights of trans children. A parliamentary commission report approved in May 2025, following the UK Cass Report, portrays gender-affirming initiatives as a threat to children's development and recommends restricting access to them.

Case volumes are rising sharply. Movilh records 3,620 national LGBTIQ+ discrimination cases in 2025, up 27.1%, the highest on record and 23% of all cases in 24 years, against 2,847 in 2024, itself up 78.7%. Regional shares should be read against that national trajectory rather than as a measure of local conditions.

Institutional hostility is also visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.
localsOnly:
Residents of Región del Maule can file anti-discrimination lawsuits under the Zamudio law, which has covered sexual orientation since 2012, gender identity since its enactment, and gender expression since 2018. Hate-motivated offences are prosecuted with sexual orientation and gender identity treated as aggravating circumstances, giving victims a defined route through the criminal courts.

Legal gender recognition for residents requires no medical evidence: name and sex can be changed on all official documents from the age of 14 by self-declaration, and intersex families can register a third sex option on a birth certificate.

Residents under 18 face a narrowing of care. The health ministry's circular N8 restricts the Gender Identity Support Program for minors, the program was removed from the 2026 budget, and legislative initiative CEI-57 targets trans children's rights, so access to gender-affirming support for young people is contracting rather than expanding.

Residents working in public institutions have a documented precedent of contesting discrimination: Isabella Panes's 2025 lawsuit against Carabineros concerns reassignment to administrative work, non-consensual exposure of her private life, and absence of institutional support.
outOfScopeNotes:
Wikipedia's Maule Region entry carries no usable finding on LGBTIQ+ or trans conditions, so all regional content rests on the Movilh national case table; the region's 2025 case share is not sourced here, only its 2024 share of 1.56%.

Implementation of the Gendarmería de Chile detention protocol inside Región del Maule is not sourced: no material records how many trans detainees the region's facilities have held, how segmented housing has been applied, or whether the standing monitoring committee has examined local compliance.

The outcome of Isabella Panes's 2025 claim against Carabineros, and whether any court outside Santiago has applied Article 390 ter of the penal code in a trans- or sexuality-motivated killing, remain unresolved in the available sources.

Whether the rollback measures (PAIG exclusion from the 2026 budget, circular N8, CEI-57) have produced denials of care to residents of Región del Maule is not sourced and should be treated as an open question.
